name: Fraxinus

project_scope.selection_mode: manifest-backed canonical learner set + Central Texas diagnostic polish
project_scope.note: All four species are canonical learner entries in data/manifest.json. F. albicans, F. pennsylvanica and F. berlandieriana currently carry project PASS range status; F. greggii remains canonical for learning with unresolved target-zone range status and is excluded from native metrics.

shared_traits: Dioecious trees/shrubs, so only female trees carry samaras
Winged samara fruit when female and mature
priority: samara wing-to-body relationship and seed-body size
leaf scar shape on recent natural leaf fall
Gregg's ash xeric shrub habit + tiny leathery foliage
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify Central Texas ashes from a single leaf silhouette. Leaflet counts overlap, leaf scars vary, and fruit is absent on male trees. Use the character hierarchy and multiple structures.

quick_key.if: Xeric shrub/small tree with tiny thick leathery leaflets, commonly 3 but up to 7; often semi-evergreen
quick_key.then: Fraxinus greggii — canonical learner; project range status remains unresolved

quick_key.if: Fruiting tree with samara body about 1 cm and wing terminal or only slightly decurrent on distal ~1/4
Fruiting tree with samara body >1.5 cm and wing decurrent on proximal body, then abruptly broadening distally; consistently 2-winged
Usually 3–5(–7) sharply serrate leaflets + samara >1.5 cm with wings gradually expanding from near base; occasional 3-winged fruits

look_here_first: First confirm opposite branching + pinnately compound leaves. On a fruiting female tree, go straight to the samara: wing attachment and seed-body size are the strongest Central Texas split. On a nonfruiting or male tree, compare the lower leaflet surface, leaflet number/margins, then several fresh leaf scars.

Small leathery leaflets; slight teeth may occur

comparison_matrix.greggii: Thick/leathery foliage; matched underside macro still needed

comparison_matrix.albicans: Depressed-obovate; upper margin shallowly concave to slightly notched, margins somewhat flaring
comparison_matrix.pennsylvanica: Shield-shaped to broadly oblong-ovate, ~3–4 mm; apex truncate to very shallowly concave

comparison_matrix.greggii: Not established as a primary project separator

comparison_matrix.albicans: Body about 1 cm; wing terminal or only slightly decurrent on distal ~1/4
comparison_matrix.pennsylvanica: Body >1.5 cm; wing decurrent from proximal ~1/4, then abruptly expanded from distal 1/4(–1/2)
comparison_matrix.berlandieriana: Body >1.5 cm; wings gradually expand from base to distal 1/3 and narrowly flange body
comparison_matrix.greggii: Small winged samara; exact matched comparison still a visual-polish target

comparison_matrix.berlandieriana: Mostly 2, but 3-winged fruits can occur among 2-winged fruits
comparison_matrix.greggii: Standard ash samara; not a primary split here

overlap_cautions: Samara form is the best Central Texas separator for mature female F. albicans, F. pennsylvanica and F. berlandieriana.
Male trees and immature trees may lack fruit entirely; then use lower leaflet surface, margins and several recent leaf scars.
Leaf scars vary. Recent natural leaf fall in late fall/winter is preferable to torn leaves, old scars or mounted-herbarium stems.
Leaflet counts overlap and should not be used alone.
Historical Texas ash / green ash / Mexican ash confusion makes multi-character confirmation especially important.
F. greggii is morphologically distinctive by xeric habit and tiny coriaceous leaflets, but its project range status remains unresolved.
